# Introduction

The question of how long people will live carries consequences that extend far beyond the domain of academic demography. Pension funds, life insurers, social security administrators, and government treasuries all make multi-decade financial commitments whose solvency depends critically on the accuracy of mortality forecasts. An underestimate of life expectancy by even a single year can translate into billions of dollars of unfunded liability for a national pension scheme; an overestimate distorts insurance pricing and misallocates public health resources. As populations across the developed world continue to age at historically unprecedented rates, the demand for mortality forecasting methods that are both accurate and robust has never been more acute.

The dominant framework for age-specific mortality forecasting over the past three decades remains the model introduced by @lee1992modeling. The Lee-Carter model decomposes the log central death rate $\ln m(x, t)$ according to the bilinear structure

$$\ln m(x, t) = \alpha_x + \beta_x \kappa_t + \varepsilon_{x,t},$$

where $\alpha_x$ captures the average age profile of mortality, $\kappa_t$ is a latent period index governing the overall level of mortality through time, $\beta_x$ quantifies the sensitivity of each age group to changes in $\kappa_t$, and $\varepsilon_{x,t}$ is a zero-mean error term. Mortality projections are then obtained by extrapolating $\kappa_t$ as a random walk with drift. The Lee-Carter model's enduring appeal stems from its parsimony and interpretability: it reduces a high-dimensional mortality surface to a single stochastic index, and the biological meaning of its components is transparent to practitioners in insurance and public policy alike.

Nevertheless, the Lee-Carter framework rests on assumptions that have attracted sustained critical attention. Most importantly, the age-sensitivity loadings $\beta_x$ are assumed to be constant over the entire estimation horizon, so that all age groups respond proportionally to the same period shock. Empirical evidence from multiple national datasets suggests that the relative pace of improvement has shifted considerably across age groups over recent decades, violating this fixed-interaction assumption. Furthermore, the model imposes a linear drift on $\kappa_t$, rendering it poorly equipped to capture structural breaks or accelerations in mortality improvement --- such as those associated with the cardiovascular revolution of the 1970s and 1980s --- without ad hoc intervention. These limitations have motivated a substantial literature exploring generalisations of the Lee-Carter framework, including the age-period-cohort extensions of @renshaw2006cohort and the multi-population models of @lilee2005coherent.

A parallel strand of research has drawn on developments in deep learning to ask whether neural networks can address the shortcomings of classical actuarial models. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, introduced by @hochreiter1997long, are a class of recurrent neural network architectures specifically designed to capture long-range temporal dependencies through gated memory cells that regulate the flow of information across time steps. Unlike autoregressive statistical models, LSTMs impose no parametric assumptions on the temporal dynamics of the series being modelled, can learn non-linear relationships between predictors and outcomes, and can in principle process the full multivariate mortality surface jointly, exploiting correlations across age groups that univariate methods discard.

Several recent contributions have assessed the applicability of these architectures to mortality data. @richman2021neural provided an influential early demonstration, replacing the random walk extrapolation of $\kappa_t$ in the Lee-Carter model with an LSTM, yielding what the present paper refers to as the kt-LSTM approach. Their results on multi-country Human Mortality Database (HMD) data indicated that recurrent networks could improve out-of-sample accuracy relative to the classical random walk specification. @perla2021time extended this line of inquiry by applying both convolutional and recurrent architectures directly to the matrix of log death rates drawn from the HMD, reporting competitive performance relative to established actuarial benchmarks across a broad cross-section of countries. @nigri2021deep proposed a hybrid strategy in which a neural network augments the Lee-Carter decomposition, learning residual structure that the bilinear model leaves unexplained. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate that deep learning methods can achieve competitive or improved accuracy relative to classical benchmarks in mortality forecasting, with gains most evident when training on rich multi-country or multi-population datasets. @booth2006lee provided an important reference point for this discussion by benchmarking a range of Lee-Carter variants across ten countries, establishing empirical baselines against which subsequent methodological proposals were evaluated.

A notable gap in this literature concerns the single-country, data-constrained setting. The favourable results reported for LSTMs have almost uniformly been obtained in regimes where the training corpus is large --- spanning many countries or very long historical series --- providing the network with the volume of observations necessary to estimate its substantial parameter count. It remains unclear whether these advantages persist when the practitioner is restricted to the mortality history of a single country over a span of decades, a scenario that is typical of the problems faced by national statistical agencies and pension fund actuaries in smaller economies. In such settings, the statistical efficiency of parsimonious classical models may reassert itself.

This paper addresses that gap directly. It presents a systematic empirical comparison of five LSTM architectures --- Vanilla LSTM, Stacked LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), CNN-LSTM, and Attention LSTM --- alongside the kt-LSTM approach of @richman2021neural, evaluated against a Lee-Carter baseline. All models are estimated and assessed on Australian male mortality data obtained from the Human Mortality Database, spanning the period 1950 to 2019. Australia was selected because it is a canonical developed-country case with a long, high-quality mortality record in the HMD, exhibits a strong and near-monotone downward trend in adult male mortality over the estimation window, and provides a single-country setting that is deliberately more constrained than the multi-country designs used in prior LSTM studies. The study does not examine female mortality or multi-country pooling; these extensions are left for future work. By holding the dataset, evaluation protocol, and error metrics constant across all methods, the study provides a controlled assessment of the conditions under which deep learning architectures add value relative to the classical benchmark.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature on classical mortality forecasting and deep learning approaches. Section 3 describes the data sources, the construction of the mortality surface, and the train/validation/test splitting procedure. Section 4 presents the Lee-Carter baseline and each of the five LSTM architectures in formal detail, together with the kt-LSTM formulation and training protocol. Section 5 reports the empirical results, including out-of-sample forecast errors, life expectancy projections, residual diagnostics, Diebold-Mariano statistical tests, kt-LSTM comparisons, and cross-validation results. Section 6 discusses the findings in the context of the existing literature and examines the conditions under which classical methods retain their advantage. Section 7 concludes.

---

# Related Work

## Classical Mortality Forecasting Models

The statistical modelling of human mortality has a history stretching back to the construction of life tables in the seventeenth century, but the modern era of stochastic mortality forecasting is most commonly traced to the landmark contribution of @lee1992modeling. Applying singular value decomposition to a matrix of logged central death rates for the United States over the twentieth century, Lee and Carter showed that a single latent index $\kappa_t$, together with age-specific loading parameters $\alpha_x$ and $\beta_x$, could account for the overwhelming majority of historical variation in age-specific mortality. Projections were obtained by modelling $\kappa_t$ as a random walk with drift, a specification that was both parsimonious and well-aligned with the secular decline in mortality observed across developed nations. The Lee-Carter model rapidly became the dominant paradigm in actuarial and demographic forecasting, and it serves as the primary benchmark in the present study.

Subsequent scholarship has sought to address well-documented limitations of the original framework. @renshaw2006cohort introduced a cohort dimension $\gamma_c$ to the bilinear Lee-Carter structure, acknowledging the strong empirical evidence that birth-cohort membership shapes mortality trajectories in ways that the original age-period specification cannot capture. Applied to England and Wales mortality data, their cohort-extended model produced materially different projections for certain age groups, highlighting that the omission of cohort effects can introduce systematic bias in long-horizon forecasts. However, the added flexibility of the Renshaw--Haberman model comes at the cost of estimation instability and convergence difficulties, particularly for shorter national series --- a problem directly relevant to the Australian data used here.

@lilee2005coherent addressed a different limitation: the tendency of independently estimated single-population Lee-Carter models to diverge when applied simultaneously to groups of related populations. By constraining multiple populations to share a common long-run factor whilst retaining population-specific terms, they ensured that the forecasted mortality trajectories of comparable nations do not diverge implausibly over long horizons. Their coherent framework has since become standard practice in multi-country actuarial analysis, though its primary relevance is to multi-population rather than single-country settings.

The empirical properties of Lee-Carter and its variants across different national contexts were systematically examined by @booth2006lee, who benchmarked the original model alongside several extensions using mortality data from ten HMD member countries. Their results confirmed that the original Lee-Carter specification is broadly competitive across a range of settings, but identified a key sensitivity to the choice of time period over which $\kappa_t$ is estimated: when the selected window spans mortality regimes with materially different rates of improvement, the extrapolated drift term may be either too optimistic or too conservative. This finding is directly pertinent to the present study, where the 1950--2004 training window for Australian males spans the post-war high-mortality era and the later phase of rapid cardiovascular improvement.

## Deep Learning for Time-Series and Mortality Forecasting

The theoretical foundations of the LSTM architectures examined in this paper rest on the seminal work of @hochreiter1997long. Earlier recurrent neural networks suffered from the vanishing and exploding gradient problems that prevented effective learning of long-range temporal dependencies: gradients either shrank to zero or grew unboundedly when backpropagated through many time steps. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber addressed this by introducing gated memory cells comprising an input gate, a forget gate, and an output gate, which allow the network to selectively retain or discard information across arbitrarily long sequences. This architectural innovation made it practical to train deep sequence models on real-world time series, and LSTM cells remain the basic building block of all five LSTM variants benchmarked in the present study.

The Attention LSTM variant examined here draws additionally on the scaled dot-product attention mechanism formalised by @vaswani2017attention. Although the Transformer architecture introduced in that work dispenses with recurrence entirely in favour of self-attention, the attention mechanism has also been incorporated into recurrent architectures, allowing the model to assign differential weight to different time steps in the input sequence when forming its prediction. In the context of mortality forecasting, this provides the model with the capacity to emphasise historically informative years --- for instance, years surrounding major structural shifts in mortality improvement --- rather than treating all lags as equally relevant.

The first systematic application of LSTM methods to mortality forecasting in the actuarial literature was undertaken by @richman2021neural, whose work is directly methodologically antecedent to the kt-LSTM approach evaluated here. Working with a large multi-country HMD corpus, Richman and Schreck replaced the Lee-Carter random walk extrapolation of $\kappa_t$ with an LSTM, demonstrating that the added flexibility of the recurrent network yielded improved out-of-sample forecast accuracy relative to the classical specification. Crucially, their gains were most pronounced when the model was trained jointly across multiple populations, exploiting cross-country commonalities in mortality dynamics. The present paper isolates the single-country case and thereby tests whether the kt-LSTM advantage survives in a data-constrained setting with no cross-population information transfer.

@perla2021time extended the deep learning approach beyond the $\kappa_t$ representation by applying convolutional and LSTM architectures directly to the full two-dimensional log-rate matrix, simultaneously learning temporal dynamics and cross-age structure from a corpus of mortality surfaces drawn from more than thirty HMD countries. Their multi-country training paradigm yielded competitive performance relative to established actuarial benchmarks and demonstrated that neural networks can exploit shared mortality patterns across heterogeneous national populations. The present study uses a comparable architecture family but limits training to a single national series, making it a more direct test of whether LSTM networks can compete with Lee-Carter in the absence of the cross-country signal that supports their performance in @perla2021time.

## Hybrid and Structured Approaches

A distinct modelling philosophy is represented by the hybrid strategy of @nigri2021deep, who augmented the Lee-Carter decomposition with a neural network trained to learn the residual structure that the bilinear model fails to capture. Applied to Italian male mortality --- a single-country setting making it the prior work most directly comparable to the present study --- this approach yielded forecasts competitive with the standard Lee-Carter model, while offering the potential to detect non-linear age interactions that the linear $\beta_x \kappa_t$ product cannot represent. The Nigri et al. results are particularly informative for the present paper: in a single-country setting where the mortality trend is strongly linear, the hybrid model did not deliver a decisive advantage over its classical counterpart, a pattern consistent with the dominance of Lee-Carter observed in the present results.

The kt-LSTM variants evaluated in this paper occupy a position between the purely classical and fully data-driven extremes. Rather than replacing the Lee-Carter framework, they retain the SVD-based decomposition and substitute only the random walk extrapolation of $\kappa_t$ with an LSTM, following the methodology of @richman2021neural. This restricted architecture preserves the interpretability of the Lee-Carter age structure whilst allowing the period index to follow a potentially non-linear trajectory. Testing these variants in a single-country context allows the present study to isolate the marginal contribution of a flexible $\kappa_t$ model from the benefits of multi-population training.

## Statistical Evaluation of Forecast Accuracy

The inferential framework used to assess whether observed differences in forecast accuracy between Lee-Carter and LSTM models are statistically meaningful is provided by @diebold1995comparing. The Diebold-Mariano test evaluates the null hypothesis that two competing forecast series have equal expected loss, without requiring either series to be nested within the other or imposing distributional assumptions on the forecast errors. Its applicability to non-nested, potentially non-normal time-series forecasts makes it the standard tool for pairwise comparisons of this kind in the econometric and actuarial forecasting literature. The life table calculations used to translate forecasted log death rates into life expectancy at birth throughout this study follow the sex-specific formula for $a_0$ --- the fraction of the first year of life lived by those who die in infancy --- specified by @andreev2015agefractions, whose sensitivity analysis established this as the preferred approach for constructing period life tables from HMD data.

The present paper occupies a specific and underexplored position in this literature. Prior deep learning mortality studies that report favourable results for LSTM or hybrid architectures have almost invariably drawn on multi-country or multi-population training corpora [@richman2021neural; @perla2021time], or have found only marginal gains over classical alternatives in single-country settings [@nigri2021deep]. The existing evidence therefore does not clearly answer whether LSTM architectures can add value over Lee-Carter when the analyst is restricted to a single country's historical record --- the most common practical constraint facing actuaries in national pension and insurance contexts. By applying five LSTM variants and two kt-LSTM families to a single country's HMD series and subjecting all pairwise comparisons to formal Diebold-Mariano testing, the present study provides the first systematic, statistically rigorous evidence on this question for Australian male mortality.

# Data

## Source and Coverage

Mortality data were obtained from the Human Mortality Database [HMD; @HMD2024, mortality.org], a curated repository of high-quality historical mortality records for countries with reliable civil registration systems. We use central death rates $m(x,t)$ for **Australian males**, spanning ages $x = 0, 1, \ldots, 99$ and calendar years $t = 1950, \ldots, 2019$, yielding a $100 \times 70$ age-by-year matrix. Central death rates are defined as the ratio of observed deaths to the central exposed-to-risk in each age-year cell.

Data are stored locally as Apache Parquet files, with each file structured as an Age $\times$ Year `pandas` DataFrame indexed by single-year age groups. The Parquet format was chosen for its efficient columnar compression and fast I/O relative to CSV, which is relevant when iterating over multiple preprocessing and training runs.

## Preprocessing

Raw central death rates span several orders of magnitude (from roughly $10^{-4}$ at young ages to $10^{-1}$ at the oldest ages), so all models operate on the natural logarithm of the central death rate:

$$y(x,t) = \ln m(x,t).$$

Log-rates are clipped to the interval $[-10,\ 1.5]$ to guard against numerical instability arising from near-zero rates in infant or young-adult age groups that can produce extreme negative values in sparse historical years.

Following log-transformation, **per-age standardisation** is applied to centre and scale each age series independently:

$$z(x,t) = \frac{y(x,t) - \hat{\mu}_x}{\hat{\sigma}_x},$$

where $\hat{\mu}_x$ and $\hat{\sigma}_x$ are the mean and standard deviation of $y(x,\cdot)$ computed **exclusively on the training set** (1950--2004). Applying the training-set statistics to validation and test years prevents data leakage and ensures the standardisation is strictly prospective.

Sequences are constructed via a **sliding window**. For direct LSTM models, the window length is $T = 20$ years: each input sample is the $20 \times 100$ matrix of standardised log-rates for a contiguous block of 20 consecutive years, with the corresponding target being the 100-dimensional log-rate vector in the immediately following year. For the kt-LSTM variants (see @sec-kt), a shorter window of $T = 10$ years is used, reflecting the lower dimensionality of the scalar $\kappa_t$ input; each sample is a 10-element sequence of standardised $\kappa_t$ values with a single next-period $\kappa_t$ target.

## Train / Validation / Test Split

Data are partitioned into three strictly non-overlapping, time-ordered segments:

| Split      | Years      | Duration | Role                                  |
|:-----------|:-----------|:---------|:--------------------------------------|
| Training   | 1950--2004 | 55 years | Parameter estimation                  |
| Validation | 2005--2009 | 5 years  | Hyperparameter tuning, early stopping |
| Test       | 2010--2019 | 10 years | Final held-out evaluation             |

: Data partition summary. {#tbl-split}

No shuffling of observations is performed across year boundaries. This strict temporal ordering is essential for mortality forecasting, where any form of future information leakage would produce optimistically biased error estimates. The 10-year test horizon (2010--2019) is standard in the actuarial and demographic literature and is long enough to assess the models' ability to extrapolate meaningful medium-term trends.

# Methods

## Lee-Carter Baseline {#sec-lc}

The Lee-Carter model [@lee1992modeling] decomposes the log central death rate matrix as:

$$\ln m(x,t) = \alpha_x + \beta_x \kappa_t + \varepsilon_{x,t},$$

where $\alpha_x$ captures the age-specific mean log-mortality, $\beta_x$ describes the age-sensitivity to the latent mortality index, and $\kappa_t$ is a scalar time trend. Parameters are estimated via **singular value decomposition (SVD)** of the centred log-rate matrix $Z = \log M - \hat{\alpha}_x \mathbf{1}^\top$, where $\hat{\alpha}_x$ is the time-average log-rate at each age. If $Z = U S V^\top$, then $\hat{\beta}_x = U_{:,1}$ (first left singular vector) and $\hat{\kappa}_t = S_1 V_{1,:}$ (first singular value times first right singular vector), so that $\hat{\beta}_x \hat{\kappa}_t^\top$ is the rank-one approximation to $Z$.

Two identification constraints are imposed: $\sum_x \beta_x = 1$ and $\sum_t \kappa_t = 0$. Because the sign of the first singular vector is arbitrary, the sign of $\sum_x \beta_x$ is checked **before** normalising: if the raw sum is negative, both $\beta_x$ and $\kappa_t$ are negated. After normalisation the sum is always $+1$ by construction, so the sign check must precede it.

The extracted $\kappa_t$ series is modelled as a random walk with drift --- equivalently, an **ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift** --- which is the canonical choice in the original Lee-Carter framework. Mortality forecasts are generated under two operational modes:

- **(a) 1-step rolling:** The Lee-Carter model is refit each year on an expanding window of all data up to year $t-1$, and a single 1-year-ahead forecast is produced. This mode mimics a real-time forecasting environment and produces the most directly comparable baseline for models evaluated on year-by-year prediction.
- **(b) Multi-step:** The model is fit once on the full training period (1950--2004) and $\kappa_t$ is extrapolated 10 years ahead via the ARIMA drift model, producing forecasts for all 10 test years simultaneously.

Period life tables are constructed using the **Andreev-Kingkade [-@andreev2015agefractions]** sex-specific formula for the fraction of the last year of life lived in the first age interval ($a_0$), ensuring demographic coherence in life expectancy calculations. For the open age interval (age 99+), we use $L_{99} = l_{99} / m_{99}$.

## LSTM Architectures {#sec-lstm}

All five direct LSTM variants share the same input shape --- $(B,\ T,\ 100)$ where $B$ is batch size, $T = 20$ is the sequence length, and 100 is the number of age groups --- and the same output shape $(B,\ 100)$. This design allows each model to learn the temporal dynamics of the complete age schedule simultaneously, exploiting cross-age correlations within each architecture's inductive bias. Hidden-layer width and other architecture-specific hyperparameters were determined by Bayesian optimisation (see @sec-training); the optimised hidden size was **256 units** for all five architectures.

**Vanilla LSTM.** The simplest architecture consists of a single LSTM layer [@hochreiter1997long] with 256 hidden units. Layer normalisation (LayerNorm) followed by dropout are applied in sequence to the LSTM output before the linear projection head maps the final hidden state $h_T \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$ to the 100-dimensional output.

**Stacked LSTM.** Three LSTM layers are stacked sequentially, each with 256 hidden units and connected via residual skip connections. Each block computes a LayerNorm-normalised sum of the LSTM output and a linear projection of the block's input, followed by dropout, before passing to the next layer. The residual connections prevent gradient degradation in deeper stacks, and the hierarchical gating allows each layer to abstract progressively longer-run temporal patterns. The final hidden state of the third block feeds a linear head.

**Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM).** A single BiLSTM layer runs one forward LSTM (256 units) and one backward LSTM (256 units) over the input sequence. Their hidden states at the final time step $t = T$ are concatenated to yield a 512-dimensional representation. LayerNorm is applied to this 512-dimensional vector, followed by dropout, before a linear head maps it to the 100 output ages. The backward pass provides the network with access to later contextual information within the input window, which can be beneficial for capturing non-monotone mortality patterns within the 20-year window.

**CNN-LSTM.** The age dimension is treated as a spatial axis and processed by two successive Conv1D layers (64 channels each, kernel size 5, ReLU activations) that extract local age-neighbourhood features before temporal modelling. A global average pool then collapses the age axis to a 64-dimensional feature vector per time step, which is fed as a sequence of length $T$ into an LSTM with 256 hidden units. This hybrid architecture exploits both the spatial smoothness of age-mortality schedules and the temporal dynamics captured by the LSTM.

**Attention LSTM.** An LSTM with 256 hidden units produces a sequence of hidden states $\{h_1, \ldots, h_T\}$. Scaled dot-product attention [@vaswani2017attention] is applied over these states using the final hidden state as a query: $q = W_q h_T \in \mathbb{R}^{256}$, attention logits $e_t = q^\top h_t / \sqrt{256}$, and attention weights $\alpha_t = \operatorname{softmax}(e_t)$. The context vector $c = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t h_t$ is a weighted summary of all $T$ hidden states, allowing the model to dynamically focus on the most informative historical years. A linear head maps $c$ to the 100-dimensional forecast.

## kt-LSTM Variants {#sec-kt}

Following the kt-LSTM approach of @richman2021neural, we additionally apply each LSTM architecture to the scalar $\kappa_t$ time series extracted from the Lee-Carter decomposition, rather than to the full age schedule directly. In this formulation, the LSTM receives **univariate** input of shape $(B,\ T,\ 1)$ --- a sequence of $T = 10$ scalar $\kappa_t$ values --- and outputs the next-period $\hat{\kappa}_{t+1}$. This dimensionality reduction from 100 to 1 is the key structural difference from the direct LSTM approach. Forecasted death rates are recovered by back-transformation:

$$\hat{m}(x,t) = \exp\!\bigl(\hat{\alpha}_x + \hat{\beta}_x \,\hat{\kappa}_t\bigr).$$

This yields five kt-LSTM variants (Kt-Vanilla, Kt-Stacked, Kt-BiLSTM, Kt-CNN-LSTM, Kt-Attention), each adapted for 1-dimensional scalar input. These variants are compared against both LC (rolling) and LC (multi-step) baselines to isolate the contribution of the LSTM temporal model from the contribution of the Lee-Carter structural decomposition.

## Training Protocol {#sec-training}

All LSTM models are trained under a common protocol summarised in @tbl-training:

| Hyperparameter          | Value                                           |
|:------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| Optimiser               | AdamW                                           |
| Initial learning rate   | Tuned per model (range $2.5\times10^{-3}$–$4.8\times10^{-3}$) |
| Weight decay            | Tuned per model (range $2\times10^{-4}$–$5\times10^{-4}$) |
| LR scheduler            | ReduceLROnPlateau (factor = 0.5, patience = 10) |
| Loss function           | MSE on standardised log-rates                   |
| Gradient clipping       | Max norm = 1.0                                  |
| Early stopping patience | 15 epochs (monitor: validation loss)            |
| Maximum epochs          | 100                                             |
| Batch size              | 32                                              |
| Random seed             | 42                                              |
| Hyperparameter search   | Optuna TPE (20 trials, 40-epoch proxy); hidden size = 256 for all models; dropout 0.2–0.4 |

: LSTM training hyperparameters. Learning rate, weight decay, hidden size, and dropout are determined per-architecture via Bayesian optimisation; all other settings are shared. {#tbl-training}

The learning rate scheduler halves the learning rate whenever validation loss fails to improve for ten consecutive epochs, preventing oscillation near convergence. Gradient clipping at a maximum $\ell_2$ norm of 1.0 mitigates exploding gradients, which are a known pathology in deep recurrent networks trained on long sequences. All stochastic operations (weight initialisation, dropout masks, data sampling) are seeded at 42 for reproducibility.

## Evaluation Metrics {#sec-metrics}

Model performance is assessed across all 100 single-year age groups and all 10 test years (2010--2019) using the following metrics:

- **RMSE** and **MAE** on $\ln m(x,t)$: standard point-forecast accuracy measures on the log-rate scale, which down-weights large absolute errors at high-mortality ages.
- **ME (Mean Error / Bias):** $\frac{1}{100 \cdot 10}\sum_{x,t}[\hat{y}(x,t) - y(x,t)]$, measuring systematic over- or under-estimation.
- **MAPE (%):** mean absolute percentage error computed on the central death rate scale (after exponentiating log-rate forecasts back to $m(x,t)$), providing a scale-free summary of relative accuracy across the age schedule.
- **$e_0$ MAE (years):** Mean absolute error of the period life expectancy at birth, computed from a period life table applied to the forecasted central death rates. This metric directly quantifies actuarial and policy relevance.
- **Diebold-Mariano (DM) test** [@diebold1995comparing]: a formal test of equal predictive accuracy between each LSTM model and the LC (1-step rolling) baseline, using **squared error loss**. Loss differentials $d_t = e_{1,t}^2 - e_{2,t}^2$ are computed at each test year $t$, where $e_{1,t}$ is the LSTM mean squared error across all 100 ages and $e_{2,t}$ is the Lee-Carter 1-step mean squared error. The null hypothesis of equal predictive accuracy is evaluated via a one-sample $t$-test on $\{d_t\}_{t=1}^{10}$, yielding statistic $DM = \bar{d} / \operatorname{SE}(\bar{d})$. A **negative** DM statistic indicates that the LSTM has *larger* squared errors than Lee-Carter --- i.e., Lee-Carter is the more accurate model. Given the short test horizon of $T = 10$ years, results should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive; the large magnitudes of the observed statistics suggest the qualitative direction of the findings is robust.
- **5-fold time-series cross-validation** on the combined training and validation period (1950--2009): folds respect temporal order (no shuffling), with five expanding training windows of 30, 35, 40, 45, and 50 years. Because Lee-Carter has no tunable hyperparameters, cross-validation is applied only to the LSTM models, where it assesses the stability of their performance rankings across different historical sub-periods.

---

# Results

Across all evaluation criteria, the Lee-Carter model with one-step rolling re-estimation is the dominant forecaster: it achieves RMSE = 0.164 and life-expectancy MAE = 0.349 years on the 2010--2019 Australian male test set, outperforming every LSTM variant by margins that are both practically large and statistically unambiguous ($p < 0.001$ on all Diebold-Mariano tests). Among direct LSTM architectures, the Stacked LSTM is the strongest performer (RMSE = 0.258, $e_0$ MAE = 1.646 years), yet it still exceeds the rolling Lee-Carter benchmark RMSE by 57% and records a life-expectancy MAE nearly five times that of the rolling Lee-Carter. The kt-LSTM framework --- which restricts LSTM learning to the scalar Lee-Carter period index $\kappa_t$ rather than the full 100-dimensional age surface --- partially closes this gap: the best kt-LSTM variant, Kt-BiLSTM with rolling re-estimation, records RMSE = 0.253 and $e_0$ MAE = 1.557 years, confirming that the structured Lee-Carter decomposition provides an effective inductive prior that mitigates the LSTM's estimation burden in small-sample settings. A further regularity across all LSTM formulations is systematic over-optimism about mortality improvement: mean errors are negative for every neural architecture, ranging from $-0.122$ (Kt-BiLSTM rolling) to $-0.284$ (direct Vanilla LSTM), whereas the rolling Lee-Carter carries a near-zero bias of $-0.016$.

---

Three patterns are immediately legible from @tbl-all-models. First, rolling estimation consistently dominates multi-step projection: in four out of five kt-LSTM architecture pairs, the rolling variant outperforms its multi-step counterpart on all metrics, mirroring the large rolling-vs-multi-step gap within Lee-Carter itself (RMSE: 0.164 vs. 0.241, a 47% increase); the sole exception is the Kt-Stacked pair where rolling and multi-step are effectively tied (RMSE 0.284 for both, differing by less than 0.001). Second, the kt-LSTM approach systematically outperforms its direct-LSTM counterparts when the same underlying architecture is used in rolling mode: Kt-BiLSTM rolling (0.253) beats direct BiLSTM (0.269), and Kt-Vanilla rolling (0.257) beats direct Vanilla LSTM (0.348). Third, the life-expectancy metric exhibits a compounding effect absent from the log-rate metrics: errors grow proportionally larger in $e_0$ terms because small biases in individual age groups accumulate across the full life table, rendering the LSTM's systematic negative ME especially costly for actuarial applications.
