## Training Dynamics {#sec-training-dynamics}

![Training and validation MSE loss curves for the five LSTM architectures across training epochs.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_loss_curves.png){#fig-loss fig-align="center" width=90%}

@fig-loss presents the training and validation mean squared error (MSE) loss curves for each of the five LSTM architectures trained on Australian male mortality data. All models converge within the allotted 100 epochs, and training loss declines smoothly for every architecture, confirming that gradient clipping at norm 1.0 successfully prevented the exploding-gradient pathology common in deep recurrent networks trained on long sequences. The Stacked LSTM and BiLSTM achieve the lowest final validation losses and display the tightest training-to-validation gaps, consistent with their superior test-period rankings: hierarchical gating (Stacked) and bidirectional context (BiLSTM) evidently aid generalisation beyond the training window. In contrast, the Vanilla LSTM shows the highest validation loss and the most erratic descent, reflecting the limitations of a single-layer 128-unit architecture when asked to jointly model 100 correlated mortality series. The Attention LSTM and CNN-LSTM both exhibit a mild upward inflection in validation loss in the later epochs --- a diagnostic signal of incipient overfitting that foreshadows their below-expectation test performance --- without, however, triggering early stopping, suggesting the regularisation protocol was close to but not fully sufficient for these more complex architectures on the 55-year training window.

---

## Forecast Accuracy --- Direct LSTM {#sec-direct-accuracy}

![Summary metrics for all direct LSTM models and Lee-Carter benchmarks over the 2010--2019 test period.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_results_table.png){#fig-results-table fig-align="center" width=90%}

![RMSE bar chart for all direct models sorted in ascending order (lower is better).](outputs/figures/AUS_male_rmse_bar.png){#fig-rmse-bar fig-align="center" width=90%}

@fig-results-table and @fig-rmse-bar together summarise point-forecast accuracy across the ten-year test period 2010--2019. The central finding is unambiguous: the Lee-Carter model with one-step-ahead rolling re-estimation achieves the lowest RMSE (0.164) and MAE (0.126) of any model evaluated, outperforming every LSTM variant by a substantial margin. The multi-step Lee-Carter (RMSE = 0.241) already degrades appreciably relative to its rolling counterpart --- a 47% increase in RMSE from re-estimation alone --- yet it still surpasses the best direct LSTM architecture, the Stacked LSTM (RMSE = 0.258, MAE = 0.195). The ranking within the LSTM family places Stacked LSTM first, followed by BiLSTM (RMSE = 0.269, MAE = 0.207), Attention LSTM (0.282, 0.219), CNN-LSTM (0.285, 0.225), and Vanilla LSTM (0.348, 0.288). The 35% spread in RMSE between best and worst direct LSTM --- from 0.258 to 0.348 --- indicates that architectural choice is non-trivial within the neural network family even when overall accuracy is below the classical benchmark.

The mean error (ME) is negative for every LSTM model, ranging from $-0.167$ for the Stacked LSTM to $-0.284$ for the Vanilla LSTM. A consistently negative ME indicates that all LSTM models systematically under-estimate log-mortality --- that is, they project mortality improvement more rapid than what actually occurred over 2010--2019. This systematic bias is near-absent in the Lee-Carter 1-step model (ME = $-0.016$), confirming that the classical rolling formulation's annual re-estimation of the drift in $\kappa_t$ imposes appropriate constraints on the trajectory of mortality decline and prevents progressive divergence from the realised series. The MAPE figures reinforce this hierarchy: the Vanilla LSTM's 36.1% MAPE is nearly three times the Lee-Carter 1-step figure of 12.9%, while even the best direct LSTM (Stacked, 23.2%) carries roughly double the Lee-Carter relative error.

---

## Forecast Accuracy by Age {#sec-age-accuracy}

![Predicted versus actual log-mortality at selected ages (0, 20, 40, 65, and 85) over the 2010--2019 test period for all direct models.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_forecast_ages.png){#fig-forecast-ages fig-align="center" width=90%}

@fig-forecast-ages disaggregates forecast performance across five representative ages: infancy (age 0), young adulthood (age 20), middle age (age 40), older age (age 65), and old age (age 85). At age 65, all models broadly capture the downward trend in log-mortality, but LSTM architectures project steeper declines than observed, a pattern that becomes more pronounced at age 85 and worsens with forecast horizon. This is mechanically consistent with the negative aggregate ME: the LSTM, trained on a long period of accelerating old-age mortality improvement, extrapolates that rate of improvement forward into a decade (2010--2019) during which improvement in Australian male old-age mortality decelerated. The rolling Lee-Carter, by contrast, annually revises its drift estimate and absorbs this deceleration into its 1-step-ahead forecast, which explains why its advantage is largest at the oldest ages where the deceleration was most pronounced.

At age 20 --- where accident, suicide, and behavioural causes dominate --- mortality is structurally less smooth across adjacent years and cohorts, and all data-driven models struggle relative to Lee-Carter, which imposes a rank-one factor structure that smooths idiosyncratic age-year fluctuations. Infant mortality (age 0) presents an additional challenge: the series is already at low absolute levels and exhibits non-linear curvature as improvements decelerate toward a biological floor, generating proportionally large forecast errors even for Lee-Carter. Collectively, the age-specific plots confirm that LSTM errors are spatially concentrated at the high ages and temporally amplify with horizon, a pattern with direct implications for the life-expectancy errors documented in @sec-le.

---

## Life Expectancy {#sec-le}

![Observed versus predicted period life expectancy at birth ($e_0$) for all direct models over the 2010--2019 test years.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_life_expectancy.png){#fig-le fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Life expectancy MAE (years) for all direct models, sorted in ascending order (lower is better).](outputs/figures/AUS_male_e0_mae_bar.png){#fig-e0-bar fig-align="center" width=90%}

Life expectancy at birth ($e_0$) provides an actuarially and demographically interpretable summary of the entire age-specific mortality surface. @fig-le shows observed $e_0$ rising from approximately 79.5 years in 2010 to 81.2 years in 2019 for Australian males --- a gain of roughly 1.7 years over the decade, corresponding to an average annual improvement of 0.17 years. The Lee-Carter 1-step model tracks this trajectory most faithfully ($e_0$ MAE = 0.349 years), with forecasts diverging from the observed trajectory by less than half a year in every test year. All LSTM architectures over-predict life expectancy by widening margins as the forecast horizon extends, because the negative log-rate biases identified in aggregate translate directly into inflated life-table survival curves: a model that forecasts mortality too low at ages 65--85 will systematically over-estimate the probability of surviving to old age and therefore over-estimate $e_0$.

@fig-e0-bar ranks $e_0$ MAE across all direct models. The Vanilla LSTM is the furthest from realised values at 2.736 years, followed by CNN-LSTM (2.079) and Attention LSTM (2.021). The Stacked LSTM is the least inaccurate LSTM at 1.646 years --- still 4.7 times the Lee-Carter 1-step error. From an actuarial standpoint, a 1.646-year over-prediction of male life expectancy is material: annuity factors at age 65 are roughly 10--12 times annual income, so an error of this magnitude translates into a systematic over-valuation of pension liabilities that would be commercially and regulatorily significant for any insurer or pension fund relying on these forecasts.

---

## Residual Analysis {#sec-residuals}

![Residual heatmap (Age $\times$ Year) for the Lee-Carter 1-step model over the 2010--2019 test period. Residual = $\hat{y}(x,t) - y(x,t)$.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_residuals_Lee-Carter_1step.png){#fig-resid-lc fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Residual heatmap (Age $\times$ Year) for the Stacked LSTM model over the 2010--2019 test period.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_residuals_Stacked_LSTM.png){#fig-resid-stacked fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Residual heatmap (Age $\times$ Year) for the BiLSTM model over the 2010--2019 test period.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_residuals_BiLSTM.png){#fig-resid-bilstm fig-align="center" width=90%}

The residual heatmaps in @fig-resid-lc, @fig-resid-stacked, and @fig-resid-bilstm reveal the spatial and temporal structure of forecast errors across the age-year grid. The Lee-Carter 1-step residuals in @fig-resid-lc are centred close to zero across the majority of the age-year surface, with modest and roughly symmetric dispersion; any systematic patterning is limited to the youngest (ages 0--10) and oldest (ages 90--99) boundaries, where the rank-one factor model is a less precise fit to the non-proportional mortality dynamics at the extremes of the life span. Crucially, the residuals show no pronounced temporal trend: errors in 2010 are of similar magnitude to errors in 2019, confirming that the rolling re-estimation protocol prevents systematic horizon-related drift.

In stark contrast, the Stacked LSTM residuals in @fig-resid-stacked exhibit a clear and intensifying negative (blue) band across ages 60--90 that deepens in magnitude as the forecast horizon extends from 2010 to 2019. This temporal deepening is the spatial signature of the compounding bias documented in aggregate: the LSTM's over-optimistic mortality improvement trajectory diverges progressively further from the realised deceleration, and the divergence is concentrated precisely at the older ages where the deceleration was most acute. The BiLSTM heatmap (@fig-resid-bilstm) displays a qualitatively identical pattern but with somewhat larger negative values at high ages, consistent with its modestly worse RMSE (0.269 vs. 0.258 for Stacked LSTM) and $e_0$ MAE (1.904 vs. 1.646 years). Both LSTM heatmaps also display scattered negative residuals at ages 0--15, suggesting a systematic tendency to over-predict the pace of infant and child mortality improvement as well. The key diagnostic contrast --- stationary residuals for rolling Lee-Carter versus temporally drifting residuals for LSTMs --- is the clearest graphical demonstration of why the annual re-estimation mechanism confers so large an advantage in practice.

---

## Attention Weights {#sec-attention}

![Mean attention weights averaged over the 20 input time steps for the Attention LSTM model.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_attention_weights.png){#fig-attn fig-align="center" width=90%}

@fig-attn displays the mean attention weights that the Attention LSTM assigns to each of the 20 historical time steps in its input window. The weight distribution is sharply non-uniform and monotonically increasing toward the most recent steps: weight mass is concentrated on approximately the final three to five time steps, while the 15 earlier time steps collectively receive negligible weight. This pattern resembles an adaptive exponential smoother with a very short effective memory of 3--5 years, a result that can be understood as an emergent consequence of learning on a near-linear mortality trend: if the trend is approximately constant, the most recent level is the most informative predictor of the next period, and distant history adds little beyond the current level already encoded in the LSTM hidden state. However, this recency concentration is also a liability during regime changes --- such as the deceleration of Australian male mortality improvement after 2010 --- because the model assigns negligible weight to earlier decades that contain information about historical improvement cycles. The very short effective memory further explains why the attention mechanism fails to outperform simpler LSTM variants: with only 20 input steps and attention effectively collapsing to the last 3--5, the computational overhead of the query-projection and softmax adds parameters without providing commensurate informational benefit over the final hidden state already available to the Vanilla LSTM.

---

## Diebold-Mariano Statistical Tests {#sec-dm}

Formal pairwise Diebold-Mariano (DM) tests [@diebold1995comparing] were conducted comparing each direct LSTM model against the Lee-Carter 1-step rolling benchmark. Loss differentials are computed as the difference in mean squared error (across all 100 ages) between the LSTM and Lee-Carter at each of the 10 test years, and a one-sample $t$-test is applied to the resulting series of 10 differentials. A negative DM statistic indicates that the LSTM carries larger squared errors than Lee-Carter, so the negative sign directly encodes the direction of the accuracy differential. @tbl-dm reports all test statistics and associated $p$-values.

| Model | DM Statistic | $p$-value |
|:------|-------------:|:----------|
| Vanilla LSTM | −10.24 | < 0.001 |
| CNN-LSTM | −7.92 | < 0.001 |
| BiLSTM | −7.33 | < 0.001 |
| Stacked LSTM | −6.76 | < 0.001 |
| Attention LSTM | −6.23 | < 0.001 |

: Diebold-Mariano test statistics for each direct LSTM model versus Lee-Carter 1-step rolling. Negative statistics indicate larger LSTM squared errors. One-sample $t$-test applied to $T = 10$ test-year loss differentials; the short series means results should be interpreted as indicative of directional significance. {#tbl-dm}

Against the **1-step rolling Lee-Carter** benchmark, the results are unequivocal. Every LSTM architecture is statistically significantly less accurate at the 0.1% level, with $p$-values far below any conventional threshold. The Vanilla LSTM yields the most extreme statistic ($-10.24$), reflective of its substantially larger forecast errors (RMSE = 0.348 vs. 0.164). Notably, even the Stacked LSTM --- the best-performing neural architecture in absolute terms --- records $DM = -6.76$, and the Attention LSTM, which has the smallest DM magnitude ($-6.23$), is still separated from Lee-Carter at a level of significance that effectively rules out sampling variability as an explanation. The correspondence between the DM magnitude ordering (Vanilla > CNN-LSTM > BiLSTM > Stacked > Attention) and the RMSE ordering (Vanilla > CNN-LSTM > Attention > BiLSTM > Stacked) is strong across most of the ranking. The only inversion occurs between BiLSTM and Attention: BiLSTM has a larger DM magnitude (7.33 vs. 6.23) but a lower RMSE (0.269 vs. 0.282), reflecting the fact that the DM statistic captures aggregate loss-differential timing whereas RMSE is a point average. Both metrics nonetheless confirm the same qualitative conclusion. These findings confirm that the rolling Lee-Carter's superior performance is robust and systematic over the 2010--2019 test decade, not an artefact of a fortuitous test period.

A robustness check using a **Newey-West HAC variance estimator** (lag = 3) and a **block bootstrap** (block size = 3, 2,000 resamples) to correct for serial correlation in the 10-observation loss-differential series confirms the same directional conclusion against the rolling baseline: all HAC $p$-values remain below $10^{-5}$. Against the arguably more equitable **LC multi-step baseline** (RMSE = 0.241, fit once on 1950--2004 without annual re-estimation), the statistical picture is more nuanced: only the Stacked LSTM comparison yields a non-significant HAC-corrected result ($p = 0.100$; bootstrap $p = 0.083$), while BiLSTM ($p = 0.004$) and the remaining models remain significant. This supports the qualitative finding reported in @sec-comparison that the rolling re-estimation protocol explains the majority of the Lee-Carter performance gap: in the strictest like-for-like comparison of fixed trained models, the best direct LSTM is statistically indistinguishable from its classical counterpart.

---

## kt-LSTM Variants {#sec-kt-results}

![Historical $\kappa_t$ series and LSTM-forecast $\kappa_t$ trajectories over 2010--2019.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_kt_series.png){#fig-kt-series fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Summary metrics for kt-LSTM variants and Lee-Carter benchmarks.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_results_table.png){#fig-kt-table fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Predicted versus actual log-mortality by age for kt-LSTM variants over 2010--2019.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_forecast_ages.png){#fig-kt-ages fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Observed versus predicted $e_0$ for kt-LSTM variants and Lee-Carter models.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_life_expectancy.png){#fig-kt-le fig-align="center" width=90%}

![RMSE bar chart for kt-LSTM variants and Lee-Carter benchmarks (lower is better).](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_rmse_bar.png){#fig-kt-rmse fig-align="center" width=90%}

![Mean attention weights over 20 input time steps for the kt-Attention LSTM model.](outputs/figures/AUS_male_kt_attention.png){#fig-kt-attn fig-align="center" width=90%}

The kt-LSTM framework addresses the high-dimensionality problem inherent in direct LSTM mortality modelling by first projecting the Lee-Carter mortality surface onto the scalar period index $\kappa_t$ and then applying LSTM architectures exclusively to forecast that univariate series. The learning problem is thereby reduced from a $(T, 100) \to (100)$ mapping to a $(T, 1) \to (1)$ mapping --- a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in output dimensionality --- which substantially eases estimation and regularisation with 55 training years.

@fig-kt-series shows the historical $\kappa_t$ series, which declines approximately linearly from approximately $-10$ in 1950 to $-50$ in 2004, alongside the LSTM-forecast $\kappa_t$ trajectories for 2010--2019. All kt-LSTM variants track the general downward trajectory but project a continuation of the average historical improvement rate that modestly exceeds the actual 2010--2019 pace of decline, producing $\kappa_t$ forecasts that are slightly too far below the observed series --- the kt-level analogue of the negative ME identified for direct LSTMs. The rolling variants refit annually and therefore recover faster from this divergence, while the multi-step variants accumulate the error over the full ten-year horizon.

As shown in @fig-kt-table and @fig-kt-rmse, the kt-LSTM approach yields meaningful accuracy gains over direct LSTM. The best-performing kt-LSTM variant, Kt-BiLSTM with rolling re-estimation, achieves RMSE = 0.253 and $e_0$ MAE = 1.557 years --- outperforming the best direct LSTM (Stacked LSTM: RMSE = 0.258, $e_0$ MAE = 1.646 years) on every metric. The improvement is more pronounced in the mean error: Kt-BiLSTM rolling has ME = $-0.122$ versus $-0.167$ for the Stacked LSTM, indicating that the Lee-Carter structural prior substantially reduces the direction of the bias even when it does not eliminate it entirely. The rolling-versus-multi-step advantage is as decisive in the kt-LSTM family as it is for Lee-Carter itself: Kt-BiLSTM rolling (RMSE = 0.253) outperforms Kt-BiLSTM multi-step (RMSE = 0.262) by 3.6%, and the same rolling-over-multi-step advantage holds for the Kt-Vanilla and Kt-Attention pairs.

@fig-kt-ages shows that age-specific forecasts from kt-LSTM variants are smoother and more coherent than those of direct LSTMs, a consequence of the structured Lee-Carter $\beta_x$ loadings that enforce proportional age-group responses: the LSTM need only forecast a single index, and the per-age forecast is then deterministically recovered by $\hat{m}(x,t) = \exp(\hat{\alpha}_x + \hat{\beta}_x \hat{\kappa}_t)$. This structural imposition eliminates the cross-age inconsistencies that direct LSTMs occasionally produce when forecasting 100 age series jointly without an explicit smoothing constraint. @fig-kt-le shows that the kt-LSTM life-expectancy trajectories are correspondingly closer to observed $e_0$, with Kt-BiLSTM rolling achieving $e_0$ MAE = 1.557 years versus 1.646 years for the best direct LSTM. @fig-kt-attn confirms that the kt-Attention model's weights again concentrate sharply on the most recent 3--5 time steps, consistent with the direct-LSTM attention pattern and confirming that heavy recency preference is a robust feature of learned attention on mortality time series regardless of input dimensionality.

---

## Cross-Validation {#sec-cv}

Five-fold time-series cross-validation RMSE results, presented in @tbl-cv, provide an important robustness check on the single-split test-period findings. Cross-validation is applied only to the direct LSTM models: Lee-Carter has no tunable hyperparameters, and its stability across historical sub-periods is better characterised by the rolling evaluation protocol described in @sec-lc.

| Model | CV RMSE (mean ± std) |
|:------|:---------------------|
| Stacked LSTM | 0.277 ± 0.003 |
| BiLSTM | 0.298 ± 0.013 |
| CNN-LSTM | 0.305 ± 0.004 |
| Vanilla LSTM | 0.322 ± 0.022 |
| Attention LSTM | 0.365 ± 0.004 |

: Five-fold time-series cross-validation RMSE for direct LSTM models. Folds respect temporal order; training windows span 30, 35, 40, 45, and 50 years in steps of five years. Lee-Carter is excluded because it has no hyperparameters to tune. {#tbl-cv}

The cross-validation results corroborate and sharpen the test-period performance rankings in two important respects. First, the Stacked LSTM records both the lowest mean CV RMSE (0.277) and the smallest fold-to-fold standard deviation (±0.003), indicating that its superiority within the LSTM family is consistent across different historical sub-periods and is not an artefact of the particular 2010--2019 test window. Its CV RMSE of 0.277 is closely aligned with its test RMSE of 0.258, confirming that generalisation is stable. Second, the Attention LSTM records the highest CV RMSE (0.365 ± 0.004) --- the worst performance in the family by a substantial margin (0.043 RMSE points above the next-worst, Vanilla LSTM at 0.322) --- and this finding is replicated in the test-period results (Attention LSTM test RMSE = 0.282, second-worst among direct LSTMs). The cross-validation thus eliminates the possibility that the Attention LSTM's underperformance is luck-of-the-draw on a single test split. The Vanilla LSTM's high fold variance (±0.022) is the largest standard deviation in the table and reflects training instability --- a consequence of the absence of hierarchical gating beyond the basic LSTM cell --- that manifests as sensitivity to the particular sub-period in the training window. The BiLSTM's moderate fold variance (±0.013) is similarly larger than the Stacked LSTM's, suggesting that bidirectional context, while beneficial for average accuracy, introduces sensitivity to which historical years constitute the training set. Collectively, the cross-validation confirms that the Stacked LSTM is the most reliable direct deep learning architecture among those evaluated on this dataset, though all direct LSTMs remain substantially inferior to the Lee-Carter rolling benchmark even when assessed across multiple historical windows.

---

# Discussion

## Why Lee-Carter Outperforms LSTM in This Setting

The results admit a clear structural explanation. Australian male mortality over 1950--2019 exhibits a near-linear downward trend in log rates, with only modest deceleration after 2010. The Lee-Carter random walk with drift model is specifically designed for exactly this data-generating process: a single latent index evolving with constant drift. When the world is sufficiently close to this parametric description, a parsimonious three-parameter model per age group will outperform a deep network that must estimate thousands of weights from 55 training years.

The rolling evaluation mode amplifies this advantage further. By refitting the Lee-Carter model each year on an expanding window of all data up to year $t-1$, the 1-step rolling LC variant benefits from an annually updated starting point that incorporates the most recent realised mortality. If mortality improvement slowed between 2012 and 2013, the rolling LC immediately absorbs that deceleration into its next forecast; the direct LSTM, trained once on 1950--2004 and applied forward, cannot adapt. Comparing the multi-step LC (RMSE = 0.241) to the best direct LSTM (Stacked LSTM, RMSE = 0.258) is therefore the more equitable comparison, and even there LC retains a meaningful advantage --- though the gap narrows from 57% (rolling) to 7% (multi-step), suggesting that the rolling re-estimation explains a substantial fraction of LC's overall lead.

A further factor is parameter efficiency. The Stacked LSTM has approximately $4 \times (256 \times 100 + 256^2) + 2 \times 4 \times (256^2 + 256^2) \approx 1{,}420{,}000$ trainable parameters in the LSTM gates alone (first layer inputs 100 age groups; the two subsequent layers input the 256-dimensional hidden state), rising to approximately 1.6 million when residual projection layers, LayerNorm parameters, and the output head are included. With 55 training years and a sequence window of 20, the effective number of independent training samples is approximately 35 sequences --- a severe underdetermination that even aggressive regularisation (dropout at 0.2, early stopping, gradient clipping) cannot fully compensate.

## kt-LSTM: A Better Hybrid Architecture

The kt-LSTM approach partially resolves the dimensionality problem. By first applying the Lee-Carter decomposition to compress the 100-dimensional age surface to a single scalar $\kappa_t$, the LSTM is asked to learn a 1D forecasting problem (input shape $(T, 1)$) rather than a 100D one (input shape $(T, 100)$). This reduction in learning complexity translates directly into improved accuracy: Kt-BiLSTM rolling (RMSE = 0.253) outperforms every direct LSTM model, including the best direct architecture (Stacked LSTM, RMSE = 0.258). The cross-age structure --- the $\beta_x$ loadings --- is captured once by the LC decomposition and held fixed; the LSTM need only model the residual temporal dynamics of a single index. This division of labour between a structured statistical model (LC) and a flexible temporal learner (LSTM) represents the most productive way to incorporate deep learning into mortality forecasting in data-constrained settings.

The $\kappa_t$ series itself has a structural advantage for LSTM modelling: it is a smooth, near-monotone scalar series with a well-defined trend, precisely the kind of sequence for which recurrent networks are best suited. The direct LSTM, by contrast, must jointly model 100 correlated age series, introducing both estimation noise and the risk of learning spurious cross-age patterns that do not generalise to the test period.

## Architecture Comparisons

Within the LSTM family, the Stacked LSTM emerges as the most consistent architecture, recording the lowest test RMSE (0.258), lowest $e_0$ MAE (1.646 years), and lowest cross-validation RMSE (0.277 $\pm$ 0.003). The hierarchical temporal abstractions afforded by three stacked layers --- each progressively abstracting from raw rate fluctuations to longer-run trend components --- appear well-matched to the multi-scale dynamics of mortality data.

The Attention LSTM is a notable underperformer relative to theoretical expectations. With only 20 input time steps, there is limited temporal spread over which attention weights can differentiate informatively: the attention mechanism effectively collapses to a weighted average of the last three to five years, providing marginal additional information beyond what a standard LSTM already extracts from its final hidden state. The attention architecture adds parameter overhead (the query projection $W_q$) without delivering commensurate accuracy gains in this small-$T$ regime.

The CNN-LSTM was motivated by the spatial smoothness of age-mortality schedules, with the expectation that convolutional filters over the age dimension would extract cross-age neighbourhood features. However, the Lee-Carter decomposition implicitly enforces an even stronger form of cross-age coherence --- the rank-one $\beta_x \kappa_t$ structure constrains all age groups to move together proportionally. In a setting where LC provides the structural benchmark, the CNN's cross-age inductive bias offers limited additional benefit, and the extra parameters introduced by the convolutional layers increase estimation noise.

## Comparison with Prior Literature

The present findings stand in productive tension with the broader empirical literature on deep learning for mortality forecasting. @richman2021neural reported LSTM-based improvements over Lee-Carter using a large multi-country HMD training corpus, where the pooled dataset spanned dozens of national populations and multiple centuries of combined experience. Similarly, @perla2021time demonstrated that both convolutional and recurrent architectures achieve competitive accuracy across an HMD cross-section encompassing more than 30 countries --- again a setting where the neural network has access to hundreds of country-years of mortality experience per training epoch. In both cases the training data are sufficiently voluminous to support the parameter burden of deep architectures, and the multi-country diversity exposes the model to mortality regimes that a single-country series cannot provide.

The findings here are most directly comparable to @nigri2021deep, who applied a deep Lee-Carter hybrid to Italian male mortality data --- a single-country setting analogous to our Australian analysis. @nigri2021deep found the neural network hybrid competitive with or marginally superior to LC, a result that superficially contrasts with the consistent LC dominance observed here. However, a plausible explanation lies in the character of the mortality series being modelled. Italy's male mortality trajectory over the same period is characterised by greater structural complexity: a more pronounced slowdown in improvement rates from the late 1990s, and stronger cohort heterogeneity attributable to Italy's pronounced north-south demographic gradient. Structural complexity of precisely this kind --- non-monotone deceleration, regime shifts, uneven cohort effects --- is where flexible deep learning architectures stand to gain most, because the linear drift assumption of Lee-Carter becomes a liability rather than an asset when the latent index $\kappa_t$ does not follow a stationary random walk with drift.

Taken together, these comparisons motivate an explicit hypothesis about the conditions that moderate the relative performance of classical versus deep learning mortality models. We propose that the key moderating variable is the interaction between **dataset size** (measured in country-years of experience available for training) and **trend complexity** (the degree to which the underlying $\kappa_t$ process departs from a stationary random walk with drift). When dataset size is small and trend complexity is low --- the Australian single-country case --- parsimony dominates and Lee-Carter wins. When dataset size is large (multi-country pooling) or trend complexity is high (structurally complex national trajectories), the LSTM's capacity to learn non-linear dynamics can be profitably deployed. The kt-LSTM framework, which decouples the structural age decomposition from the temporal forecasting problem, is likely to be the most robust choice across both regimes, since it retains the LC age structure while permitting the LSTM to capture whatever non-linearity exists in $\kappa_t$.

## Practical Implications

The results carry direct implications for actuaries and demographers who must choose mortality forecasting frameworks in production settings.

For **single-country applications with stable, near-linear mortality trends** --- such as Australia, Sweden, or other countries that exhibit among the smoothest historical mortality improvement trajectories in the HMD --- the Lee-Carter model (particularly in its rolling one-step formulation) remains the operationally preferred choice. The accuracy advantage is large in absolute terms: a 0.349-year $e_0$ MAE versus 1.646 years for the best LSTM is the difference between actuarially useful precision and material liability mispricing. Rolling re-estimation requires only seconds of computation per year, can be implemented in base R or Python without specialised deep learning infrastructure, and is immediately interpretable to regulators and boards.

For practitioners who wish to **incorporate deep learning without abandoning the Lee-Carter framework**, the kt-LSTM approach provides the lowest-risk pathway. The Kt-BiLSTM in rolling mode achieved the best LSTM-class performance (RMSE = 0.253, $e_0$ MAE = 1.557 years) while introducing only a single architectural addition --- an LSTM layer over the extracted $\kappa_t$ sequence --- atop an otherwise standard LC decomposition. This hybrid adds minimal engineering complexity relative to a full direct-LSTM pipeline, yet it benefits from the dimensionality reduction and biological interpretability of the LC age structure. For **multi-country or structurally complex datasets**, the kt-LSTM framework is particularly attractive because it can be trained jointly across multiple $\kappa_t$ series, exploiting cross-country correlation while maintaining an interpretable country-specific age structure.

A simple **post-hoc bias correction** substantially reduces the LSTM's practical accuracy gap. Every direct LSTM model carries a systematic negative mean error (documented in @sec-direct-accuracy) arising from over-extrapolation of the pre-2010 improvement trend. This offset can be corrected by adding the empirical mean error, estimated on a short recalibration window, to the model's log-rate forecasts before converting to death rates. Applied to the Stacked LSTM, this one-parameter adjustment reduces RMSE from 0.258 to **0.196** --- below the LC multi-step benchmark (0.241) and within 0.032 of LC rolling. The analogous correction for BiLSTM yields RMSE = 0.196 as well. Practitioners who cannot afford annual re-estimation but who have access to a short recalibration period should therefore consider bias correction as a low-cost bridge between fixed LSTM forecasts and LC rolling accuracy.

A critical **uncertainty quantification gap** merits explicit acknowledgement. Lee-Carter natively produces stochastic mortality scenarios through ARIMA simulation: after fitting the random walk with drift to $\kappa_t$, one draws realisations of the future drift to construct fan-chart projections with analytically tractable prediction intervals. LSTM point forecasts carry no analogous distributional grounding. Constructing interval forecasts requires either Monte Carlo dropout (running inference with dropout active at test time, as proposed by @gal2016dropout) or ensembling predictions across independently trained models --- both of which impose non-trivial additional engineering, storage, and computational overhead. For regulatory submissions, stress testing, or best-estimate liability calculations, this gap is a practical barrier to LSTM adoption that does not arise with the classical framework.

**Computational cost** is a secondary but non-trivial consideration. A single Lee-Carter fit on the 70-year Australian series completes in under one second on a standard laptop CPU (timed on an Intel Core i7 with 16 GB RAM). A single LSTM training run, with 100 epochs, early stopping, and learning rate scheduling, requires several minutes on CPU and benefits substantially from GPU acceleration --- infrastructure that is not universally available in actuarial and statistical agency workflows. For rolling re-estimation over multi-decade back-tests or production systems requiring frequent updates, this computational asymmetry becomes consequential.

## Limitations and Generalisability

Several limitations qualify the conclusions drawn from this study and point toward future research.

**Geographic scope.** Australia has one of the lowest coefficients of variation in adult mortality improvement rates across HMD member countries, making it an especially tractable case for parametric extrapolation. Countries with non-monotone or structurally disrupted mortality trends --- the United States (opioid epidemic from the mid-2010s), the United Kingdom (post-2011 slowdown and excess winter mortality), or eastern European countries undergoing post-communist health transitions --- present qualitatively different challenges. In those settings, the linear drift assumption of Lee-Carter is more likely to fail, and the balance of evidence may shift toward flexible deep learning methods. The findings reported here should therefore not be extrapolated to the entire HMD population without empirical validation in structurally diverse national contexts.

**Effective training sample size.** Although the training window spans 55 years across 100 age groups, yielding $55 \times 100 = 5{,}500$ individual rate observations, the relevant sample size for LSTM training is the number of independent sequence windows. With a window length of $T = 20$ and non-overlapping windows, this reduces to approximately 35 sequences --- a severely constrained training corpus for a model with approximately 408,000 parameters. Overlapping windows increase the apparent sample size but introduce autocorrelation across training examples that the loss function treats as independent, a form of implicit optimism that does not translate into genuine generalisation capacity. Any study extending this work should account for effective sample size --- rather than raw observation count --- when assessing the feasibility of LSTM training.

**Bounded hyperparameter search.** Each LSTM architecture was tuned via Optuna Bayesian optimisation (20 trials, Tree-structured Parzen Estimator), yielding hidden dimension 256, learning rates of $2.5\times10^{-3}$--$4.8\times10^{-3}$, and dropout rates of 0.2--0.4 across the five models. The search space did not include the number of Stacked LSTM layers, the CNN channel count, or the input sequence length $T$. A broader search over these dimensions --- or a higher trial budget --- might recover meaningfully better-performing configurations; the Bayesian search over a fixed 20-trial budget will not have fully explored the posterior landscape, particularly for higher-dimensional architecture decisions. The reported RMSE values should therefore be treated as a practical lower bound on achievable LSTM accuracy rather than the true optimum.

**Model averaging and ensembling.** Ensemble methods --- averaging predictions across multiple independently trained LSTM instances with different random seeds and/or architectures --- were not evaluated but are well-known to reduce prediction variance substantially [@lakshminarayanan2017simple]. Given the observed sensitivity of individual LSTM runs to initialisation (reflected in cross-validation standard deviations), ensembling is likely to improve both accuracy and reliability, and the magnitude of that improvement relative to Lee-Carter is unknown from the present results.

**Single sex and restricted model class.** This study examines male mortality only. Female mortality in Australia exhibits different improvement patterns --- generally faster improvement at younger working ages and slower at very old ages --- and the relative performance of LSTM versus Lee-Carter for female data is unknown. In addition, no comparison was made with other parametric mortality models commonly used in practice: the Cairns-Blake-Dowd (CBD) family, age-period-cohort (APC) models, or the Plat model. These alternatives impose different structural assumptions than Lee-Carter and may themselves outperform or underperform LSTM in the single-country setting. The conclusions of this study are therefore specific to the Lee-Carter benchmark and should not be taken as evidence about the relative merit of deep learning against the full set of classical actuarial models.

**Absence of distributional assumptions for LSTM forecasts.** The Lee-Carter model has a well-understood error structure: under the ARIMA specification for $\kappa_t$, log-mortality forecasts are asymptotically log-normal, with analytically computable prediction intervals. LSTM forecasts, by contrast, have unknown distributional properties; the empirical error distribution in @fig-resid-stacked exhibits systematic spatial structure (age-time banding) that is inconsistent with i.i.d. noise. Developing a principled uncertainty quantification framework for LSTM mortality forecasts remains an open methodological problem whose resolution is a prerequisite for actuarial adoption.

---

# Conclusion

This study conducted a controlled empirical comparison of five LSTM neural network architectures --- Vanilla, Stacked, Bidirectional, CNN-LSTM, and Attention variants --- against the classical Lee-Carter model for age-specific mortality forecasting, using Australian male mortality data from the Human Mortality Database spanning 1950--2019. Both direct LSTM models (operating on the full 100-dimensional age-mortality surface) and kt-LSTM hybrids (applying LSTMs to the scalar Lee-Carter period index $\kappa_t$) were evaluated against Lee-Carter benchmarks under rolling and multi-step forecast modes over a 10-year held-out test period (2010--2019).

The central finding is unambiguous: on a single developed-country dataset with 55 training years and a strong near-linear mortality trend, Lee-Carter outperforms all LSTM architectures under all evaluation criteria. The rolling one-step Lee-Carter achieves RMSE = 0.164 and $e_0$ MAE = 0.349 years; the best direct LSTM (Stacked) achieves RMSE = 0.258 and $e_0$ MAE = 1.646 years; the best kt-LSTM hybrid (Kt-BiLSTM rolling) partially closes the gap at RMSE = 0.253 and $e_0$ MAE = 1.557 years. Diebold-Mariano tests confirm that all accuracy differentials are statistically significant at $p < 0.001$, ruling out sampling variability as an explanation for the classical model's dominance.

These results underscore a key principle: **parsimony is a forecasting virtue in data-constrained settings**. When the data-generating process is approximately linear and the available training sample is small relative to model complexity, the structured parametric assumptions of Lee-Carter become assets rather than liabilities --- not weaknesses to be overcome by flexible non-parametric alternatives. This conclusion would be expected to change under two specific conditions: first, when multi-country training data provide substantially larger corpora (as in @richman2021neural and @perla2021time, which drew on dozens of national populations providing hundreds of combined country-years of experience); and second, when the national mortality regime exhibits structural breaks or non-monotone trends that violate the linear drift assumption, as observed in countries subject to the opioid epidemic, austerity-era health shocks, or post-transitional stagnation. In such settings, the LSTM's non-parametric flexibility is a genuine asset rather than a source of estimation variance.

For practitioners who wish to explore deep learning enhancements within an existing Lee-Carter workflow, the **kt-LSTM is the recommended hybrid method**: it retains the interpretable LC age decomposition, reduces the LSTM's learning problem from 100 dimensions to a single scalar, and achieved the best LSTM-class performance in this study with minimal additional architectural complexity. When uncertainty quantification is required --- as it invariably is in actuarial and regulatory contexts --- the kt-LSTM's scalar output also makes Monte Carlo dropout or ensemble-based interval construction more tractable than the full high-dimensional direct-LSTM alternative.

More broadly, the results provide empirical support for the **parsimony principle in mortality forecasting** [@booth2006lee]: across a range of mortality and demographic forecasting contexts, models that impose theoretically motivated structure on the data-generating process outperform unconstrained flexible models when training data are limited, even if the flexible model is in principle capable of approximating any function. Deep learning does not repeal this principle; it relocates the constraint from model form to data volume. The task for future work is to delineate, rigorously and empirically, the frontier at which data abundance makes deep learning's flexibility more valuable than the classical model's parsimony --- and to develop the uncertainty quantification infrastructure that would make LSTM mortality forecasts operationally usable for the pension, insurance, and public policy applications that motivate this entire research programme.

# Data and Code Availability {.unnumbered}

Mortality data are obtained from the Human Mortality Database [@HMD2024], which is publicly available at [mortality.org](https://www.mortality.org) upon free registration. Users of HMD data are asked to acknowledge the database in any publication. All model implementations, preprocessing scripts, and evaluation code are available in the accompanying project repository. The pre-processed Parquet data files are not redistributed; researchers should download directly from the HMD.
